frictionVectors.title: European Gas Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains significant leverage through pipeline and LNG exports, but European diversification efforts and pricing pressure could reduce long-term dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Border Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali and Libya raises security costs and complicates Algeria's efforts to protect southern infrastructure and preserve diplomatic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European partners, and China are competing for influence around the Lobito rail and Atlantic minerals corridor, increasing Luanda's strategic leverage but also external dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining or volatile oil output limits fiscal autonomy, while foreign operators and creditors retain significant influence over offshore production and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Pipeline Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Niger over border access and crude exports through the Seme-Kpodji corridor threaten port revenues and expose Benin's infrastructure to regional political retaliation.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Insurgent Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the northern borders is increasing pressure for foreign security assistance while testing Benin's control over transport routes and protected areas.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong negotiating power through Debswana, but its diamond economy remains exposed to De Beers restructuring, weaker global demand, and external marketing channels.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Electricity imports and chronic water constraints limit industrial autonomy and complicate plans to process minerals domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pursuing greater state participation and tighter control over gold, creating friction with foreign mining companies and increasing uncertainty over investment conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and AES Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Closer security ties with Russia and fellow Alliance of Sahel States governments reduce Western influence but may deepen dependence on opaque security and commodity networks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control and transparency in nickel, rare-earth and gold projects, but limited fiscal and technical capacity leaves room for foreign operators to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda security standoff
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border support continue to divert resources toward security and complicate regional trade and infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign basing and port access
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde uses partnerships with the United States, Europe and China to strengthen maritime security and logistics, while balancing concerns over strategic dependence and sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries enforcement gap
frictionVectors.details: Limited patrol capacity leaves the archipelago vulnerable to illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, weakening control over a vital national resource.

highlights: Oil and mining control remains centralized

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain central to roads, dams and other major projects, creating financing and maintenance dependencies even as Yaounde seeks greater local participation.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and resource corridors
frictionVectors.details: Violence in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts transport, agriculture and investment while weakening state control around major commercial corridors and extractive sites.

frictionVectors.title: Russian mining and security presence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel and mining interests remain influential, giving Bangui battlefield support but limiting transparency and weakening sovereign control over gold and diamond revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Regional corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on roads through Cameroon and neighboring states exposes fuel, food and mineral exports to insecurity, border closures and competing external influence.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state relies heavily on hydrocarbons and foreign technical and marketing partners, leaving public finances and national bargaining power exposed to production shocks and external commercial terms.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover and foreign partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict has intensified refugee, arms and border-security pressures, while Chad balances relations with Gulf actors, France and other partners around strategic logistics and security access.

frictionVectors.title: FRENCH CONTROL OF MAYOTTE
frictionVectors.details: France’s administration of Mayotte remains a core sovereignty grievance and complicates Comoros’ control over migration, maritime space, and regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: LIMITED MARITIME CAPACITY
frictionVectors.details: Weak coastguard and port infrastructure leave Comoros reliant on external partners for maritime security, fisheries oversight, and trade connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: MINING LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain major influence in copper and cobalt through contracts and infrastructure-linked investments, while Western governments seek greater access to strategic minerals.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN SECURITY CRISIS
frictionVectors.details: M23-related instability and alleged external support continue to undermine Kinshasa’s sovereignty in the east and threaten transport corridors serving mineral production.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on offshore oil leaves fiscal sovereignty exposed to price volatility and limits diversification, while foreign operators retain substantial technical and commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and construction projects deepen connectivity but can increase creditor dependence and reduce transparency over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE CHAIN
frictionVectors.details: Côte d’Ivoire is expanding domestic processing and regulatory control, but foreign traders and global price-setting mechanisms still capture much of the sector’s value.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY PARTNERSHIPS
frictionVectors.details: Growing cooperation with France, the United States, and regional partners improves coastal and counterterrorism capacity while creating sensitivities over strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: BASES AND STRATEGIC RENT
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of American, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generates revenue but makes Djibouti’s sovereignty highly dependent on external security competition.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Control of major logistics infrastructure and debt obligations linked to foreign-backed projects create persistent concerns over asset leverage and long-term fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Suez security
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and instability around the Red Sea threaten Suez Canal revenues and raise maritime-security costs. Egypt is balancing naval coordination with major external partners while preserving control over the waterway.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions, Gulf capital, and foreign investment support macroeconomic stability but constrain policy autonomy. Strategic infrastructure and port assets remain exposed to long-term external participation.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling production and limited domestic technical capacity intensify reliance on foreign operators and regional processing arrangements. Revenue volatility is weakening the state's room for autonomous development planning.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea maritime security
frictionVectors.details: Offshore energy infrastructure remains vulnerable to piracy, illegal fishing, and contested maritime activity. Equatorial Guinea depends on external naval and commercial partners to protect its resource zone.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard currency but leave extraction, technology, and market access heavily dependent on foreign firms. Sanctions risk and limited transparency complicate the state's ability to convert resources into broad-based sovereign capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline attracts attention from Gulf states, Turkey, and other external powers seeking military and commercial access. Asmara uses this competition to preserve autonomy but faces pressure over ports and regional alignments.

frictionVectors.title: Economic dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Imports, electricity links, logistics, and regional customs arrangements leave Eswatini highly exposed to South African economic and political conditions. This limits independent control over critical infrastructure and supply security.

frictionVectors.title: Resource and governance pressure
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, and light manufacturing depend on external markets and investors, while domestic political tensions can deter diversification. International scrutiny over governance adds friction to access to development finance.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy and GERD
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's control over its electricity strategy but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan. External mediation and regional security calculations continue to shape operating room around the dam.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt distress and foreign-exchange shortages increase reliance on IMF support, bilateral creditors, and Chinese-linked infrastructure finance. Conflict-related destruction and insecurity further weaken state control over transport, energy, and agricultural assets.

frictionVectors.title: French commercial legacy
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is seeking greater state control and local processing in oil, mining, and forestry, challenging long-standing French-linked business influence. The transition is managed but could unsettle established concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Manganese and timber exports remain dependent on constrained rail and port infrastructure. External financing and operators retain leverage over the logistics chain.

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for trade routes, food supplies, energy connectivity, and security cooperation. This creates practical stability but limits independent control over transport and border policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and foreign-linked fishing activity continues to strain coastal resource governance. Limited monitoring and enforcement reduce the state's ability to capture the full value of its maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and water loss
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage farmland and waterways while exposing weaknesses in licensing and enforcement. Foreign-backed gold networks and informal operators dilute state control over production and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals leverage
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is pursuing local processing and tighter terms for lithium and other strategic minerals, but fiscal dependence and infrastructure needs strengthen the bargaining position of external investors and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: The rail, port, and mine complex is increasing Guinea's strategic importance while binding it to large Chinese, Singaporean, and other foreign capital interests. The government seeks domestic gains, but financing and technical dependence remain substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Political exclusion and contracts
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses mining control to build legitimacy while postponing or restricting political competition. Opaque contract enforcement and concentrated executive power raise risks of elite capture and external rent-seeking.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew dependency
frictionVectors.details: Cashews dominate export earnings, but processing remains limited and farmers capture a small share of final value. Foreign traders and regional intermediaries retain substantial control over the supply chain.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore and fisheries pressure
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime enforcement leaves fisheries and prospective offshore resources vulnerable to foreign exploitation. Political instability and limited administrative capacity constrain the state's ability to regulate concessions and collect revenue.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and External Debt Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal consolidation and debt-service demands constrain Nairobi's policy space. Western lenders, bondholders, and Chinese creditors all retain leverage over infrastructure and budget priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Mombasa Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port expansion and transport corridors attract Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interest. Kenya is diversifying partners, but financing terms and regional security risks complicate control of logistics assets.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenues but deepen structural dependence on Pretoria. Dam construction, compensation, and project financing remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Mining Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains exposed to external trade preferences, foreign-owned textile production, and diamond investment cycles. Limited domestic processing reduces Lesotho's ability to retain value from its resources.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to exports, but foreign operators capture substantial capital and value-chain benefits. Weak local processing and governance capacity limit Liberia's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport of Monrovia Competition
frictionVectors.details: The port is critical to trade and regional connectivity, drawing interest from international logistics and shipping firms. Concession terms and security cooperation require careful balancing to avoid excessive external control.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest access to terminals, fields, and revenue flows through national institutions. Production remains vulnerable to shutdowns, blockades, and opaque political bargains.

frictionVectors.title: External Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, Gulf states, Egypt, and European governments retain significant influence through security, migration, and energy relationships. This external competition limits unified Libyan control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, Cobalt, and Ilmenite Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining projects dominate key export minerals, while Madagascar captures limited downstream processing and fiscal value. Commodity-price exposure and contract disputes remain persistent sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and weak roads increase dependence on foreign capital for basic infrastructure. Mining enclaves can operate with greater capacity than surrounding communities, intensifying distributional and political tensions.

highlights: Energy and fertilizer dependence remain acute

frictionVectors.title: External debt and IMF conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Malawi’s fiscal space is heavily constrained by debt restructuring and reliance on IMF and donor support. Currency pressure and import shortages limit the government’s ability to direct strategic resources independently.

frictionVectors.title: Power and fuel infrastructure bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fuel, fertilizer, and unreliable electricity exposes Malawi to external price shocks. Foreign-backed energy and mining projects are increasingly important but offer limited near-term sovereign leverage.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over strategic mining

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater state participation and revenue from gold mining, creating sustained tension with foreign operators and investors. Production and investment remain vulnerable to regulatory uncertainty and insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bamako relies increasingly on Russian-linked security personnel and political support as relations with France and regional organizations deteriorate. This improves regime protection but reduces strategic autonomy and raises risks of opaque concessions.

highlights: Gas exports create a new strategic revenue base
Mining and logistics remain externally dominated

frictionVectors.title: GTA offshore gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and international partners strengthens Mauritania’s fiscal prospects but leaves technology, financing, and marketing largely external. Cross-border governance and revenue-sharing remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and corridor concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains reliant on iron ore exports and the single Nouadhibou-Zouérate rail corridor. Chinese and other foreign capital is important for expansion, while weak diversification limits sovereign bargaining power.

highlights: Indian Ocean alignment remains carefully balanced

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty and base politics
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to seek a durable settlement over the Chagos Archipelago while balancing sovereignty claims with the strategic role of the Diego Garcia facility. Negotiations involving the United Kingdom and United States carry major diplomatic and security consequences.

frictionVectors.title: External exposure in finance and logistics
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius benefits from Indian, Chinese, British, and Gulf investment but remains exposed to shifts in offshore-finance rules and global shipping conditions. Its diversified economy gives it more policy flexibility than most regional peers.

highlights: Industrial sovereignty expands through green investment
Western Sahara remains the central strategic fault line

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is converting diplomatic recognition of its autonomy plan into stronger economic and security partnerships, while the Polisario dispute continues to shape relations with Algeria and the European Union. Phosphate, fisheries, and infrastructure projects remain politically contested.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and U.S. investment supports ports, automobiles, renewables, and defense-industrial ambitions. These partnerships strengthen Morocco’s capabilities but create competition over supply chains, technology access, and long-term control of critical assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique's largest gas projects remain dependent on foreign operators, lenders, and security guarantees. Delays and contract structures limit near-term domestic control over export revenues and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency and External Security
frictionVectors.details: The Cabo Delgado insurgency continues to make strategic energy corridors reliant on foreign military and private-security support. This weakens state control over territory surrounding major gas assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Emerging Energy
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil discoveries and green-hydrogen plans offer Namibia leverage but require large foreign investments, technology, and export infrastructure. Negotiating local-content and revenue terms is becoming a central sovereignty test.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, and Gulf actors are competing for access to uranium, lithium, rare earths, and Walvis Bay logistics. Namibia retains policy space, but infrastructure finance could create long-term external dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are seeking greater state control and better terms in mining, especially uranium. Production uncertainty, sanctions exposure, and weak administrative capacity constrain how quickly that agenda can deliver sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The post-Western security realignment increases reliance on Russia and neighboring Sahel partners for regime protection. New security dependencies may replace, rather than eliminate, external influence over strategic infrastructure and resources.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Control
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and aging pipelines continue to reduce public capture of petroleum value. Greater domestic refining could improve sovereignty, but upstream operations remain exposed to multinational and security-sector bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Grid Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria needs foreign capital and technical partners for power, transport, and gas infrastructure while managing debt and currency pressure. Financing terms can restrict policy autonomy if reforms are driven primarily by external creditors.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda is building value from tantalum, tin, tungsten, and gold, but international scrutiny over mineral traceability and alleged links to eastern Congo remains intense. Sanctions or due-diligence barriers could constrain access to premium markets.

frictionVectors.title: DRC Conflict and External Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with the Democratic Republic of the Congo expose Rwanda to diplomatic pressure, trade disruption, and possible restrictions on security cooperation. Reliance on foreign aid, investment, and strategic partnerships amplifies the cost of regional isolation.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore licensing uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in São Tomé and Príncipe's offshore blocks remains constrained by limited state capacity, uncertain commercial prospects, and investor caution. The government is balancing petroleum ambitions against environmental and fiscal risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign access to fisheries
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on external partners for maritime surveillance, port services, and fishing-related revenue. Limited enforcement capacity leaves its tuna resources vulnerable to opaque licensing and illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers Dakar greater leverage over revenues, but efforts to audit or revise legacy contracts risk disputes with international operators and lenders. Managing expectations over local content and public spending will be central to sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure financing from Gulf, Chinese, European, and multilateral partners is expanding connectivity while creating competing influence channels. Dakar must prevent strategic ports, logistics corridors, and energy assets from becoming locked into externally controlled concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles retains strong institutional capacity relative to its size, but tuna access agreements and distant-water fleets remain sensitive sovereignty issues. Weak transparency or enforcement could reduce the state's share of marine value.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, the United States, and European partners all seek maritime access, surveillance cooperation, or infrastructure influence. Victoria is using diversification to preserve autonomy, but dependence on external security and finance remains structural.

highlights: Mining reform targets local value capture

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-controlled mineral chains
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, bauxite, gold, and diamond operations remain dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented logistics. Government efforts to increase royalties, local processing, and community benefits face bargaining pressure from investors and commodity cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-resources exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external partners remain important to mining, roads, energy, and port development. Limited fiscal space increases the risk that infrastructure agreements prioritize export corridors over broad domestic industrialization.

frictionVectors.title: Port and security patronage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, and other partners compete for influence over ports, maritime security, and logistics while federal and regional authorities retain overlapping powers. External support strengthens state capacity but can fragment national control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore hydrocarbons and fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore oil and gas blocks, alongside valuable fisheries, are vulnerable to disputed licensing, weak enforcement, and illegal foreign extraction. Al-Shabaab activity and fragmented governance continue to limit Somalia's ability to convert maritime resources into sovereign revenue.

highlights: Grid and logistics remain binding constraints

frictionVectors.title: Mining ownership and beneficiation
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is pressing for local processing and greater value capture from platinum-group metals, manganese, and other critical minerals. Tensions persist with multinational miners over regulation, investment conditions, and infrastructure reliability.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and freight bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Power-system weakness and rail-port congestion continue to reduce sovereign control over export capacity. Private-sector investment and foreign technology are increasingly necessary to stabilize strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the state’s lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on Sudanese pipelines and export terminals, leaving its principal revenue stream exposed to Sudan’s war and cross-border bargaining. Chinese, regional, and international commercial actors retain significant leverage over production and transit.

frictionVectors.title: Armed control of resource corridors
frictionVectors.details: Localized armed groups and political factions contest roads, oil areas, and border trade routes. Weak institutions limit the government’s ability to convert resource wealth into nationally controlled infrastructure.

highlights: Gold remains the principal hard-currency asset

frictionVectors.title: Gold and wartime external finance
frictionVectors.details: Competing military authorities and armed networks depend heavily on gold production and trading channels. Foreign states and commercial intermediaries influence supply routes, procurement, and access to hard currency.

frictionVectors.title: Port and pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The Red Sea coast, Port Sudan, and oil-export infrastructure are strategic pressure points in the conflict. External security partnerships and disruptions to transport corridors directly constrain Sudan’s sovereign economic options.

highlights: Resource nationalism is becoming more institutionalized
Transport and LNG ambitions expand strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining and project control
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking stronger fiscal, local-content, and domestic-benefit terms from international gas developers. Delays and negotiations over the LNG framework reflect the government’s effort to retain greater sovereign control without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The expansion of Dar es Salaam and regional rail corridors is attracting Gulf, Chinese, and other foreign investment. These partnerships improve connectivity but create long-term questions over concessions, debt exposure, and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign influence over port logistics
frictionVectors.details: Lomé’s role as a transshipment and regional trade hub brings substantial foreign capital and commercial influence. Dependence on external operators, shipping networks, and security partnerships limits fully autonomous control of the corridor.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector value capture
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain central to Togo’s resource strategy, but financing, technology, and downstream processing rely heavily on external partners. The government faces pressure to expand domestic beneficiation while maintaining investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Leverage
frictionVectors.details: European funding and political engagement remain tied to Tunisia's efforts to curb irregular migration, creating pressure on domestic policy and border sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak domestic production and reliance on imported hydrocarbons leave Tunisia vulnerable to external price shocks and financing constraints.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline strengthens Uganda's export prospects but leaves the project exposed to Western environmental criticism, financing restrictions, and dependence on Tanzanian transit.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Funded Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external lenders remain important for transport and energy projects, increasing repayment pressure and limiting fiscal room for independent development choices.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Western, Chinese, and Gulf investors are competing for copper and cobalt access, giving Zambia leverage but also risking limited local processing and value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Debt Restructuring Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt-restructuring conditions and creditor negotiations continue to constrain public investment, while transport corridors remain vulnerable to external financing priorities.

highlights: Lithium Controls Seek More Local Value

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Concession Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export restrictions and beneficiation demands to capture more value from lithium and other minerals, but foreign capital and technology remain indispensable.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and External Finance
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, restricted market access, and chronic currency instability raise dependence on opaque intermediaries and discourage transparent long-term infrastructure investment.
